{"id": "20:47/q20", "question": "How is 'peace upon whoever follows guidance' understood?", "turns_on": "Whether salām is safety, an earthly salutation, a future angelic salutation, or an inward state.", "positions": [{"id": "20:47/q20/p1", "position": "It promises safety from God's displeasure and punishment, in this life and the next, to those who follow guidance.", "reasons": "Zajjāj rejects a greeting because this is not the start of an encounter; Bagawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Nasafī, and Ibn ʿĀshūr agree. Wāḥidī allows ʿAṭāʾ's blessing report to mean this or greeting. Rāzī infers safety for the knower of God who follows guidance. Ālūsī and al-Baḥr argue safety in both lives already gives encouragement and warning alongside 20:48. Ibn ʿĀshūr adds honor and says no addressee is named; his comparison is the Heraclius letter's 'accept Islam and be safe.' Study Quran adds peace from God, angels, and believers."}, {"id": "20:47/q20/p2", "position": "It is a closing or farewell greeting intended to invite Pharaoh toward guidance.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya's reported group separates it from the preceding speech and says it reproaches Pharaoh. Rāzī reports God's order to say it; Samīn gives both syntactic readings. Bursevī says the definite article gives general peace and the greeting implies safety in both abodes. Abū Ḥayyān treats it as a closing salutation, and Ṭabāṭabāʾī as a farewell-like summary. Iṣlāḥī connects its sincerity and subtle warning to 20:44. Ibn Kathīr explicitly addresses the conditional peace to Pharaoh."}, {"id": "20:47/q20/p3", "position": "It is the angels' and Paradise keepers' greeting to the guided.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī contrasts Paradise's greeting with the Fire keepers' rebuke, an implied promise of the Garden matching the exhortation and 20:48. Bayḍāwī and Nasafī record this alternative."}, {"id": "20:47/q20/p4", "position": "Inwardly, peace is freedom from defects and attachments and influx of spiritual light.", "reasons": "Qāshānī reads the promise as a spiritual state."}]}
{"id": "20:47/q21", "question": "Who is the peace directed to?", "turns_on": "Whether the saying offers a present conditional invitation or describes a future greeting.", "positions": [{"id": "20:47/q21/p1", "position": "It applies generally to anyone following guidance, with Pharaoh included if he accepts.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says the repeated address reproaches Pharaoh, then broadens the promise to everyone; refusal exposes him to destruction. Ibn Kathīr addresses the possibility directly to Pharaoh. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the indirect promise invites him. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says avoiding direct address undercuts Pharaoh's self-importance."}, {"id": "20:47/q21/p2", "position": "It is especially the guided recipients of an angelic greeting in Paradise.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī identifies angels and Paradise keepers as speakers; others report this reading."}]}
{"id": "20:47/q22", "question": "What does following guidance entail?", "turns_on": "Whether the expression describes outward faith and obedience or its inward enabling condition.", "positions": [{"id": "20:47/q22/p1", "position": "It means believing in God, submitting to His message and affirming His signs in obedience.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Ibn al-Jawzī specify faith in God; Thaʿlabī says submission. Bursevī says affirming the signs brought by prophets, whether bodily following or conforming obedience, comparing 2:38."}, {"id": "20:47/q22/p2", "position": "Inwardly, it requires prior divine guidance and an illuminated heart that follows proof and divine light.", "reasons": "Al-Wāsiṭī says God first guides the follower in every state. Qushayrī says gnosis illumines the receptive heart while ignorance blocks hearing. Qāshānī describes adherence to proof and divine light."}]}
{"id": "20:47/q23", "question": "How does على function with السلام?", "turns_on": "Whether على must be read as equivalent to لام.", "positions": [{"id": "20:47/q23/p1", "position": "It may carry the sense of لِـ, so peace or safety is for the guided.", "reasons": "Rāzī cites 13:25, 41:46, 17:7 for comparable usage; Qurṭubī reports Farrāʾ. Bursevī compares 40:52. Ālūsī says prepositions can exchange functions and notes stylistic correspondence with العذاب على من كذب in 20:48."}, {"id": "20:47/q23/p2", "position": "Its ordinary force already suits established security, so replacing it with لِـ is unnecessary.", "reasons": "Samīn rejects the recourse to lām; Ibn ʿĀshūr says على conveys security settled upon the follower."}]}
{"id": "20:47/q24", "question": "How does the peace statement relate to the next warning?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:47/q24/p1", "position": "It pairs promise for guidance with threat for denial, encouraging Pharaoh to believe.", "reasons": "Jishumī contrasts safety in both worlds with punishment of those denying the messengers; Qushayrī says prophets promise reward and warn of punishment though deferred details are unknown. Zamakhsharī sees Paradise and Fire guardians; Ālūsī and al-Baḥr say safety versus punishment in both lives already explains the pair. Ibn ʿĀshūr links ʿalā with the next verse, and Iṣlāḥī sees a subtle warning."}]}
{"id": "20:47/q25", "question": "How is the formula used when addressing non-Muslims?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:47/q25/p1", "position": "It serves as a conditional greeting in speech or writing to non-Muslims.", "reasons": "Yahyā reports its use in letters to polytheists. Ibn Kathīr recounts the Prophet's letter to Heraclius, followed by an invitation to Islam, safety and doubled reward; he also recounts Muhammad's answer to Musaylimah's claim of shared prophethood and land, citing 7:128. Ibn ʿAbbās transmits the Heraclius letter in Durr. Qatāda prescribes the formula on entering homes of People of the Book. Abū Ḥayyān concludes ordinary greetings to unbelievers should be avoided; Ālūsī cites both the letter and Qatāda."}]}
{"id": "20:47/q26", "question": "What spiritual mission is read in the release command?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:47/q26/p1", "position": "The soul should cease enslaving its animal powers and release them toward divine presence and true knowledge.", "reasons": "Qāshānī contrasts holy light with sensory pleasure and worldly adornment."}]}
{"id": "20:47/q27", "question": "What wider purpose did Moses' mission serve?", "turns_on": "Whether political emancipation exhausts the prophetic mission.", "positions": [{"id": "20:47/q27/p1", "position": "It joined faith in God to ending oppression and rescuing Israel; Egypt's ruler was also called to monotheism.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says Moses' primary mission was to establish Israel as an independent nation with reforming law, rather than legislate for Egyptians; he still summoned Pharaoh's people to monotheism to oppose wrong and secure release, citing 17:104 and 79:17."}, {"id": "20:47/q27/p2", "position": "It was merely a nationalist campaign for freedom.", "reasons": ""}]}
{"id": "20:47/q28", "question": "How does the message balance gentleness and firmness?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:47/q28/p1", "position": "The message begins with gentle invitation yet speaks firmly against tyranny and Pharaoh's false power.", "reasons": "Rāzī lists four forceful elements: a king must submit, surrender the labor on which his power rests, end abuse, and accept the sign; he says gentleness comes first, then firmness when obstinacy appears. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says truthful directness avoids both harshness and flattery. Iṣlāḥī connects sincere sympathy to the gentle-speech instruction in 20:44."}]}
{"id": "20:47/q29", "question": "What does God's gentleness toward Pharaoh imply?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:47/q29/p1", "position": "If God treats a claimant to divinity gently, His gentleness toward affirming, repentant seekers is greater.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh makes the comparison; Abū al-Qāsim al-Ḥusayn extends it from opponents, idolaters, sinners and the proud to lovers, confessors, repenters and seekers of forgiveness."}]}
{"id": "20:47/q30", "question": "What does Israel's long suffering show about divine punishment?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:47/q30/p1", "position": "God may grant an oppressor time before painfully seizing him, then rescue those he oppressed.", "reasons": "Qushayrī draws this pattern from Israel's prolonged suffering under Pharaoh and eventual rescue."}]}
{"id": "20:47/q31", "question": "What immediate punishments may fall on a person?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:47/q31/p1", "position": "Punishment varies by station and can take the form of a hardened heart, impeded obedience, or loss of wealth and life.", "reasons": "Qushayrī says its kind and degree correspond to what is due."}]}
{"id": "20:47/q32", "question": "What happened when Moses and Aaron sought entry to Pharaoh?", "turns_on": "The differing accounts of their arrival, delay, and admission.", "positions": [{"id": "20:47/q32/p1", "position": "They waited at Pharaoh's door until an obstacle was lifted and he admitted them.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr reports Ibn ʿAbbās's ḥadīth of al-Futūn: they waited without permission for a time before a severe barrier was lifted."}, {"id": "20:47/q32/p2", "position": "They waited at the palace for two years before a court entertainer told Pharaoh.", "reasons": "Ibn Isḥāq says nobody dared inform Pharaoh; Pharaoh summoned them, and Moses identified himself as a messenger Pharaoh recognized."}, {"id": "20:47/q32/p3", "position": "They came by night after Moses reunited with his family; staff-knocking brought them before Pharaoh.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī says Moses met his mother and Aaron, arranged Aaron's help, knocked with the staff, was called mad by guards, and received Pharaoh's order to admit them."}]}

{"id": "20:47/q34", "question": "How is Isrāʾīl pronounced in the reported variant?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:47/q34/p1", "position": "The variant handles the hamza between rāʾ and yāʾ differently while keeping the full syllabic length.", "reasons": "Qirāʾāt ER attributes this variant to HzT."}]}
{"id": "20:48/q01", "question": "Whose speech is this warning, and where does the dictated message end?", "turns_on": "Whether the messengers' continuing speech after the peace formula is still God's dictated instruction.", "positions": [{"id": "20:48/q01/p1", "position": "It continues the speech God instructed Moses and Aaron to deliver; the peace and warning are part of the dictated message.", "reasons": "Yahya says the revelation statement continues the preceding speech. Ibn Ashur cites the transition to Pharaoh's question and says this stretch was absent from earlier suras. Alusi argues that their speech continues after the peace formula, so both sentences are dictated and the latter explains the warning."}, {"id": "20:48/q01/p2", "position": "The dictated message ends with the sign; Moses and Aaron add the promise and warning themselves.", "reasons": "Alusi reports this as the view of some, with reference to 20:47."}]}
{"id": "20:48/q02", "question": "Why introduce the warning as revelation to the messengers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:48/q02/p1", "position": "It delivers a general, indirect warning to Pharaoh gently, without making the messengers seem to threaten him personally.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says it warns before Pharaoh's disbelief and lets the message be completed before his response. Islahi says they report God's warning rather than impose punishment themselves, preventing a claim of personal affront. Baydawi says the explicit emphatic threat is useful and important at the start and suits what follows; Bursevi calls the threat gentle. Tabatabai says the required message remains truthful without flattery or deference to Pharaoh's false power and pride."}]}
{"id": "20:48/q03", "question": "What does revelation mean here, and how did it reach Moses and Aaron?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:48/q03/p1", "position": "Waḥy is swift communication; here Moses received it through Gabriel, and Aaron through Gabriel and Moses.", "reasons": "Bursevi gives the original sense as a swift sign or communication and lists secret speech through Gabriel, inspiration, and dream as possible forms of waḥy."}]}
{"id": "20:48/q04", "question": "Why is the revealer unnamed in the passive أُوحِيَ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:48/q04/p1", "position": "Omitting God's name forestalls Pharaoh's rash irreverence; it honors God and belittles the addressee.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan expects Pharaoh to respond irreverently if God is named; al-Samin adds that the omission honors God while diminishing Pharaoh."}]}
{"id": "20:48/q05", "question": "What grammatical role does أَنَّ الْعَذَابَ عَلَىٰ مَنْ كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ have?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:48/q05/p1", "position": "The أن clause is nominative as the نائب فاعل of passive أُوحِيَ.", "reasons": "Al-Samin says it replaces the subject suppressed by the passive verb."}]}
{"id": "20:48/q06", "question": "What does the word الْعَذَابَ mean in Arabic?", "turns_on": "The first account defines the threatened suffering; Ibn Faris gives the word's original sense.", "positions": [{"id": "20:48/q06/p1", "position": "It is pain whose suffering persists, here the punishment threatened against deniers who turn away.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi gives the continuing-pain sense and applies it to this verse."}, {"id": "20:48/q06/p2", "position": "Its original Arabic sense is striking or beating.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi transmits this etymology from Ibn Faris."}]}
{"id": "20:48/q07", "question": "Which punishment does the warning encompass?", "turns_on": "Whether punishment is read as worldly and afterlife retribution or as an inward condition.", "positions": [{"id": "20:48/q07/p1", "position": "It includes punishment in this world and the next, with everlasting punishment in the next life.", "reasons": "Qurtubi specifies worldly ruin and eternal Hell; Nasafi, Bursevi, Alusi, Study Quran, and Ibn Ashur include this world and the afterlife. Bursevi says finite suffering is negligible beside everlasting suffering and compares the scope with all peace; Ibn Ashur cites 79:25–26."}, {"id": "20:48/q07/p2", "position": "It is punishment in nature's hell and matter's abyss.", "reasons": "Qashani gives this inward interpretation for whoever opposes and turns away."}]}
{"id": "20:48/q08", "question": "How broad is the definite expression الْعَذَابَ, and can believers be punished?", "turns_on": "Whether the definite article covers every instance of punishment, everlasting punishment, or simply punishment generically; whether finite punishment counts beside everlasting safety.", "positions": [{"id": "20:48/q08/p1", "position": "The expression confines all punishment to deniers, so believers receive no punishment at all.", "reasons": "Wahidi takes the unqualified generic word to imply that the believing affirmer has no punishment. Alusi reports the Murji'ah inference that only unbelievers are punished; Alusi challenges that inference."}, {"id": "20:48/q08/p2", "position": "The generic or universal expression rules out everlasting punishment for believers, although finite punishment can occur.", "reasons": "Razi says the definite article may be generic or universal and that everlasting safety renders a finite punishment negligible. Bursevi likewise compares finite and everlasting suffering. Alusi says the article may designate a particular or everlasting punishment, or use hyperbolic generality compatible with finite punishment before endless safety; he rejects the inference that believers can never be punished."}, {"id": "20:48/q08/p3", "position": "The definite article is generic, effectively saying that punishment awaits whoever denies.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur compares the definite expression to an indefinite phrase and makes no categorical claim here about believers' finite punishment."}]}
{"id": "20:48/q09", "question": "Who is threatened, and what do denying and turning away involve?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:48/q09/p1", "position": "The warning targets whoever rejects God's signs, prophets, message, or faith and turns away from belief or obedience.", "reasons": "Muqatil specifies denial of God's oneness and turning from it. Qatada, via Yahya, Tabari, and Durr, specifies denial of God's signs or Book and abandonment of obedience. Tabari adds the call to oneness, obedience, and answering messengers; turning away is from truth. Tha'labi, Wahidi, Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Qurtubi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Alusi, and Study Quran identify the denied prophets, their message, signs, or faith. Ibn Kathir distinguishes inward denial from outward turning and cites 79:37–39, 92:14–16, and 75:31–32. Bursevi says denial may be by speech or deed, and turning away rejects signs and follows desire. Islahi supplies the omitted objects as their prophethood and guidance; Tabatabai includes signs and the true call. Biqai stresses that the wording covers every denier and deserter, its nominal construction making the punishment established and enduring."}]}
{"id": "20:48/q10", "question": "How does تَوَلَّىٰ express turning away?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:48/q10/p1", "position": "It can be transitive or take an understood ʿan, expressing withdrawal and abandonment of closeness.", "reasons": "Bursevi says the act consists in refusing the signs and following desire."}]}
{"id": "20:48/q11", "question": "Why are the objects of كَذَّبَ and تَوَلَّىٰ unstated?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:48/q11/p1", "position": "They are understood as the messengers' prophethood and guidance; leaving them unstated avoids wounding Pharaoh's ego.", "reasons": "Islahi connects the omission with the generally phrased warning."}]}
{"id": "20:48/q12", "question": "Why is the warning phrased generally rather than addressed to Pharaoh?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:48/q12/p1", "position": "It lets the warning reach Pharaoh without a direct insult, while implying his error and modeling proper address.", "reasons": "Islahi says a general formulation spares Pharaoh's ego. Biqai says shifting speech away from him signals that he is astray and a denier and models etiquette. Tabatabai says neither peace nor threat directly addresses him, undermining his self-importance before God's encompassing might, with 20:46 in view."}]}
{"id": "20:48/q13", "question": "How does the warning relate to the preceding peace for the guided?", "turns_on": "Whether the preceding salām is a separate greeting or part of the report of revealed safety for the guided.", "positions": [{"id": "20:48/q13/p1", "position": "It explains that the guided are safe because punishment falls on those who deny and turn away.", "reasons": "Tabrisi says the following statement clarifies that guided followers escape punishment; Tabatabai says the revelation explains the limitation of peace to the guided. {"id": "20:48/q14", "question": "Why has this verse been called especially hopeful for believers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:48/q14/p1", "position": "It assigns punishment to deniers who turn away, leaving monotheists or believers safe from that threat.", "reasons": "Tha'labi cites an unnamed tafsir, Wahidi and Nasafi call it among the most hopeful verses, Qurṭubi and Abu Hayyan transmit Ibn Abbas's judgment, Burhan reports another proposed hopeful verse, and Itqan cites al-Kirmani. Nasafi says peace is assigned to believers and punishment to deniers, with no third category; Ibn Abbas says believers neither deny nor turn away. {"id": "20:48/q15", "question": "What task and signs frame Moses and Aaron's delivery of the warning?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:48/q15/p1", "position": "God supported their mission with signs, and they went to Pharaoh to announce that they were God's messengers.", "reasons": "Qushayri says a messenger needs a clear sign proving the prophetic claim, although signs only strengthened proof against a spiritually blind audience. Tha'labi says Moses' hand emerged from his shirt bright as the sun and Pharaoh did not see the staff until the festival. Abu Hayyan names staff and hand as the signs and explains their attribution to both messengers although one performed them. Durr reports Moses' fear over a killing and speech impediment, his request for Aaron's support, Aaron's summons, their wait outside Pharaoh's court, and Pharaoh's question about their Lord. Tabrisi notes the narrative omits the transition in which they went and conveyed God's command."}]}
{"id": "20:48/q16", "question": "What other warnings or moral lessons are placed beside this verse?", "turns_on": "These are separate surrounding moral observations rather than competing interpretations.", "positions": [{"id": "20:48/q16/p1", "position": "The messengers' commands and prohibitions are paired with promise and threat.", "reasons": "Jishumi states this pairing."}, {"id": "20:48/q16/p2", "position": "Distorting scripture or religion and promoting falsehood is a grave sin.", "reasons": "Jishumi warns against following that path."}, {"id": "20:48/q16/p3", "position": "Preferring worldly life to religion is condemned.", "reasons": "Jishumi warns against acting likewise."}, {"id": "20:48/q16/p4", "position": "A dying Muʿawiya urged detachment from worldly life after condemning corruption and contrasting wrongdoers with persecuted believers.", "reasons": "Baqillani transmits his sermon after Quraysh rejoiced at his impending death; he distinguished powerless wrongdoers, armed predators, religious hypocrites, and false ascetics."}]}
{"id": "20:48/q17", "question": "What is the broader approach to knowing a verse's occasion of revelation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:48/q17/p1", "position": "Its story and circumstances are needed for interpretation, and occasion claims require reliable witness reports and caution.", "reasons": "Wahidi says the Quranic sciences are vast, his earlier compilations cover much of them, and he wrote a beginner's guide because people neglect them. He requires reports from witnesses who knew and investigated the circumstances, notes predecessors' caution, cites the Prophet through Ibn Abbas warning that uninformed Quran claims or deliberate lies about him merit Fire, and cites Ubayda telling Ibn Sirin to fear God because the witnesses had passed away."}]}
{"id": "20:48/q18", "question": "How may individual Arabic consonants and letter names be pronounced?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:48/q18/p1", "position": "A consonant uttered alone takes a supporting sound, and letter names are expanded into pronounceable noun forms.", "reasons": "Sibawayh reports al-Khalil's supporting hāʾ for a moving consonant, removed in connected speech. An alif can play the same role: ألا تا and بلى فا stand for longer commands, supported by rajaz. An initial silent consonant needs connecting alif, as in ابن and اسم. Once a supported consonant is a name, hāʾ drops and an underlying deleted letter supplies a triliteral pattern; kasra expands with yāʾ as in في, ḍamma with waw as in لو، هو، أو, and fatḥa with alif as in ما، لا. Conventional قاف and باء name letters in noun forms, unlike sound imitations غاق and قب. For bāʾ as a man's name, he gives إب in pause and آب in connection, allowing the connecting alif to fall."}]}
{"id": "20:48/q19", "question": "How should a letter named from a word be formed?", "turns_on": "Whether the letter's source or the preceding vowel governs its name.", "positions": [{"id": "20:48/q19/p1", "position": "Its name follows its source word.", "reasons": "Al-Khalil gives ضاء from ضرب, ضي from ضراب, and ضو from ضحى; Sibawayh also records some speakers calling the bāʾ from ضرب رب while intending ʿayn."}, {"id": "20:48/q19/p2", "position": "Its name follows the vowel of the immediately preceding letter.", "reasons": "Sibawayh reports this from opponents of al-Khalil."}]}
{"id": "20:48/q20", "question": "What is the status of alif-lām and connecting alif in Arabic?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:48/q20/p1", "position": "Alif-lām is one connected particle, and connecting alif can be distinguished from interrogative alif.", "reasons": "Al-Khalil compares the article with قد and أن rather than the separate interrogative hamza; it can detach from a noun like هل، قد، سوف, with a poetic recollection of قد as evidence. Sibawayh shows connecting alif in أيم الله from إيم الله and ليم الله, while interrogative آلرجل takes an open alif to avoid confusion."}]}
{"id": "20:48/q21", "question": "How do articulated consonants and vowels work, and can sounded letters be eternal?", "turns_on": "Whether the succession of audible letters entails origination or the letters' essences and divine perfection establish eternity.", "positions": [{"id": "20:48/q21/p1", "position": "Sounds and letters are sequential, and speech made of them is originated rather than eternal.", "reasons": "Razi distinguishes a moving consonant from bodily motion: it follows a silent articulation with a sound. Vowels are reducible portions of voiced sound; prolonging them yields sound. A consonant precedes its dependent vowel, avoiding circularity. In a word earlier letters cease before later ones arise; simultaneous triliteral letters could not choose among six orders."}, {"id": "20:48/q21/p2", "position": "Letters and God's speech are eternal.", "reasons": "Razi reports proponents arguing that letters have distinct essences which cannot vanish, that God's speech is a perfection whose absence would imply deficiency and a transition to perfection, and that oath law ties hearing God's speech to hearing these letters."}]}
{"id": "20:48/q22", "question": "Can jinn know the unseen?", "turns_on": "Whether the Solomon report rules out jinn knowledge or they may acquire it through heavenly hearing or unknown means; Razi questions the certainty of these proposals.", "positions": [{"id": "20:48/q22/p1", "position": "They cannot know it.", "reasons": "Razi cites their remaining under Solomon after his death without knowing that he had died."}, {"id": "20:48/q22/p2", "position": "They can know it by approaching the heavens and overhearing angels.", "reasons": "Razi reports this explanation from some."}, {"id": "20:48/q22/p3", "position": "They can know it by other means unknown to humans.", "reasons": "Razi reports this separate proposal."}, {"id": "20:48/q22/p4", "position": "The realities of such questions are known only to God.", "reasons": "Razi cautions that proposed answers are conjecture and speculation."}]}
{"id": "20:48/q23", "question": "What harms are included in seeking refuge from God?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:48/q23/p1", "position": "It covers countless false beliefs, sins, bodily harms, fears, and worldly afflictions; one should seek God for protection from all of them.", "reasons": "Razi divides spiritual and bodily evils. False beliefs are without number; he counts seventy-two deviant Muslim sects and at least seven hundred outside.
